title: The Impact of Heatwaves on Mortality and Morbidity and the Associated Vulnerability Factors: A Systematic Review
journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (per PubMed record)
variables: Heatwave exposure; all-cause/cause-specific mortality and morbidity; sensitivity-based vulnerability factors (age, sex, SES, comorbidity, rurality)
key_findings: Heatwave events increase mortality and morbidity incidence; elderly, children, low-SES groups, people with cardiopulmonary/renal/mental disease and rural residents show heightened vulnerability
limitations: Narrative synthesis across heterogeneous heatwave definitions and outcome metrics; risk-of-bias varies by included study; no pooled effect size for India specifically
rag_summary: Systematic review (32 studies, 2012-2022) confirming heatwaves raise mortality/morbidity, with elderly, low-SES, rural and comorbid populations most vulnerable; supports personalized-risk vulnerability weighting in SwasthyaSathi.
keywords: heatwave; mortality; morbidity; vulnerability; systematic review; elderly; comorbidity

title: Vulnerability to Heat-related Mortality: A Systematic Review, Meta-analysis, and Meta-regression Analysis
variables: Ambient temperature/heat waves; mortality; subgroup vulnerability (age >65, >75, low SES)
key_findings: Strongest evidence of heat-vulnerability found for elderly (>65, >75 years) and low socioeconomic-status groups; evidence for other subgroups (children, people living alone) inconclusive
limitations: Heterogeneity between subgroup definitions across studies; RRR meta-regression sensitive to study selection; causal pathways not established for all subgroups
rag_summary: Meta-analysis/meta-regression showing the elderly and low-SES individuals carry the strongest evidence for heat-mortality vulnerability, while evidence for children/isolated individuals remains inconclusive — useful for calibrating age/SES risk weights without over-claiming for under-evidenced groups.
keywords: heat-related mortality; vulnerability; meta-regression; elderly; socioeconomic status

title: Association between ambient temperature and heat waves with mortality in South Asia: Systematic review and meta-analysis
study_type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (Navigation Guide methodology)
population: 27 studies (qualitative synthesis), 5 in meta-analysis; South Asia, 1990-2020
variables: Ambient temperature; heat waves; all-cause mortality
key_findings: U-shaped mortality-temperature relationship in South Asia with increased mortality at both high and low temperatures; statistically significant heat-wave association reported in a subset of studies
limitations: Only 5 of 27 eligible studies could be pooled quantitatively; substantial regional heterogeneity within South Asia; India-specific effect sizes not separately reported in abstract
rag_summary: South-Asia-specific systematic review/meta-analysis (highly relevant to an India-based tool) confirming a U-shaped temperature-mortality relationship, with heat waves associated with excess all-cause mortality across the region.
keywords: South Asia; India; heat wave; ambient temperature; mortality; meta-analysis

title: Impact of heatwave on mortality under different heatwave definitions: A systematic review and meta-analysis
variables: Heatwave definition (percentile/duration thresholds); total and cardiorespiratory mortality
key_findings: Heatwave-related mortality risk increased 3-16% depending on the temperature-percentile/duration threshold used to define a heatwave; magnitude of effect is definition-dependent
limitations: No universally consistent heatwave definition exists, complicating cross-study comparison; effect sizes not directly transferable to non-included regions
rag_summary: Meta-analysis showing that the mortality risk attributed to a 'heatwave' varies substantially (3-16% increase) depending on which percentile/duration threshold is used to define it — important for how SwasthyaSathi calibrates its own heat-alert thresholds without overstating precision.
keywords: heatwave definition; mortality risk; percentile threshold; meta-analysis

title: Association of heat and cold waves with cause-specific mortality in Iran: a systematic review and meta-analysis
variables: Heat/cold waves; all-cause, cardiovascular, respiratory mortality; age and sex subgroups
key_findings: Heat waves significantly increased all-cause, cardiovascular and respiratory mortality; elderly (>65) showed larger effect sizes than younger groups
limitations: Findings specific to Iranian climate/health-system context; cross-country generalizability uncertain
rag_summary: Regional (Iran) meta-analysis reinforcing that heat waves elevate cardiovascular and respiratory mortality more than all-cause mortality broadly, and that elderly populations bear a disproportionate share of this risk.
keywords: heat wave; cold wave; cardiovascular mortality; respiratory mortality; Iran

title: Assessing Heat-Related Mortality Risks among Rural Populations: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Epidemiological Evidence
journal: International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health (per PMC record)
population: 14 studies, 7 countries, 4 continents, rural settings; 11 in meta-analysis
variables: Daily mean temperature; all-cause and cardiovascular mortality in rural areas
key_findings: Pooled RR = 1.030 (95% CI 1.013-1.048) for all-cause mortality and RR = 1.111 (95% CI 1.045-1.181) for cardiovascular mortality per 1°C increase; rural excess risk not smaller than urban
limitations: Only 14 eligible studies found globally on rural heat mortality — an evidence gap; heterogeneous rural definitions across countries
rag_summary: Quantifies heat-mortality dose-response in rural populations: roughly 3% higher all-cause mortality and 11% higher cardiovascular mortality per 1°C rise, relevant for SwasthyaSathi's rural/outdoor-worker risk messaging.
keywords: rural; heat-related mortality; cardiovascular; dose-response; meta-analysis

title: Mortality, morbidity and healthcare costs of short-term high temperatures and heatwaves exposure in older populations: a global systematic review and meta-analysis
study_type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42023423311, Navigation Guide framework)
population: 623 eligible studies (of 21,610 screened), 6 continents, 305 locations, older adults
variables: Short-term high temperature/heatwave exposure; ICD-10 cause-specific mortality, morbidity, healthcare costs in older adults
key_findings: Confirms elevated cardiovascular, respiratory and cerebrovascular mortality/morbidity in older adults during heat exposure; identifies additional risks (self-harm, digestive disease, COPD, asthma, dementia) not previously synthesized
limitations: Very recent/large review; effect heterogeneity across climate zones; healthcare-cost estimates vary by country income level
rag_summary: Large-scale (623-study) 2026 meta-analysis specifically on older adults, confirming heat raises risk not just for cardiovascular/respiratory disease but also self-harm, COPD, and dementia-related morbidity — supports broader elderly risk-flagging beyond classic heatstroke.
keywords: older adults; heatwave; healthcare costs; ICD-10; dementia; cardiovascular

title: A physiological approach for assessing human survivability and liveability to heat in a changing climate
authors: Jane W. Baldwin; Coen Bongers; Kristie L. Ebi; et al.
population: Modeled young and older adults, male/female, sun/shade scenarios
variables: Wet-bulb temperature (Tw); age; sex; sun exposure; survivability and liveability limits
key_findings: Physiology-based survivability limits are 0.9-13.1°C lower than the classic 35°C Tw threshold, especially in hot-dry conditions and for older females (7.2-13.1°C lower)
limitations: Modeling study, not direct clinical outcome data; assumes idealized conditions (shade, hydration); real-world acclimatization and clothing vary
rag_summary: Shows the traditional 35°C wet-bulb survivability limit substantially underestimates risk, especially for older adults and in dry heat — SwasthyaSathi's environmental risk fusion should not treat 35°C Tw as a universal 'safe' cutoff.
keywords: wet-bulb temperature; survivability; heat physiology; older adults; climate change

title: Mapping Human Survivability at Extreme Wet-Bulb Temperatures 32-35°C
population: 60 young males, 48 young females; controlled chamber study
variables: Wet-bulb temperature 32-35°C; metabolic rate; prolonged heat exposure tolerance
key_findings: Empirical human chamber data extends prior modeling; critical Tw thresholds for uncompensable heat stress observed within 24.1-34.6°C range depending on conditions
limitations: PREPRINT — not yet peer-reviewed; young/healthy sample only, not generalizable to elderly or comorbid populations
rag_summary: Preprint (flag as not yet peer-reviewed) providing rare empirical (not just modeled) human data on survivable wet-bulb temperature ranges — should be cited as preliminary evidence only.
keywords: wet-bulb temperature; human chamber study; heat tolerance; preprint

title: Validating new limits for human thermoregulation
variables: Wet-bulb temperature; thermoregulatory failure threshold
key_findings: Laboratory studies suggest humans cannot effectively thermoregulate at wet-bulb temperatures above 26-31°C — considerably lower than the widely publicized 35°C threshold
limitations: Based on limited laboratory exposure durations; population-specific thresholds (age, fitness) not fully resolved
rag_summary: Reinforces that safe wet-bulb thermoregulation may fail well below 35°C (as low as 26-31°C), a key caution against using 35°C as SwasthyaSathi's critical heat threshold.
keywords: thermoregulation; wet-bulb temperature; heat limits

title: Is a wet-bulb temperature of 35°C the correct threshold for human survivability?
population: Modeled acclimatized, young, healthy adult outdoors in shade
variables: Wet-bulb temperature; heat index; outdoor habitability thresholds
key_findings: Heat-index-based model provides two-threshold system (vs single Tw value); questions whether 35°C Tw over- or under-estimates true survivability depending on wind/radiative conditions
limitations: Focused on healthy, acclimatized adults — does not address vulnerable subgroups directly; outdoor/shade-only scenario
rag_summary: Provides an alternative heat-index-based framework (beyond single wet-bulb value) for assessing outdoor heat habitability, useful context for how 'feels-like' temperature relates to physiological risk.
keywords: heat index; wet-bulb temperature; outdoor habitability; climate

title: Short-Term PM2.5 Exposure and Cardiovascular Mortality: A Global Exposure-Response Analysis to Inform Alert Thresholds
journal: Journal of the American College of Cardiology (JACC)
study_type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (3-stage meta-regression, spline functions)
population: 100 epidemiologic studies, 123 effect estimates, global, up to May 2025
variables: Short-term PM2.5 exposure; cardiovascular mortality; nonlinear exposure-response
key_findings: Nonlinear exposure-response relationship confirmed; proposed alert threshold of 136 µg/m3 could prevent 73.2% of attributable deaths while affecting only 32% of at-risk person-days
limitations: Global pooled function may not reflect India-specific baseline pollution/comorbidity context; alert-threshold trade-off is a policy choice, not a clinical cutoff
rag_summary: Most current (2025) global meta-analysis establishing a nonlinear PM2.5-cardiovascular mortality curve and a candidate short-term alert threshold (136 µg/m3) — directly relevant to SwasthyaSathi's AQI-based risk fusion engine.
keywords: PM2.5; cardiovascular mortality; exposure-response; alert threshold; air quality

title: Short-term exposure to particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), and ozone (O3) and all-cause and cause-specific mortality: Systematic review and meta-analysis
population: Observational time-series studies, outdoor air pollution, non-occupational
variables: PM10, PM2.5, NO2, O3; all-cause, cardiovascular, respiratory, cerebrovascular mortality
key_findings: Positive association found between short-term PM10/PM2.5/NO2/O3 exposure and all-cause mortality; PM10 and PM2.5 also linked to cardiovascular, respiratory and cerebrovascular mortality; robust to sensitivity analyses
limitations: Effect sizes per 10 µg/m3 increase may not linearly extrapolate to India's higher ambient pollution levels
rag_summary: Establishes high-confidence, multi-pollutant (PM10, PM2.5, NO2, O3) short-term mortality associations for all-cause and cause-specific outcomes — core evidence for the AQI component of the risk engine.
keywords: PM10; PM2.5; NO2; ozone; short-term exposure; mortality

title: Long-term exposure to particulate matter on cardiovascular and respiratory diseases in low- and middle-income countries: A systematic review and meta-analysis
population: 38 cohort/case-control studies, low- and middle-income countries
variables: PM1, PM2.5, PM10; cardiovascular and respiratory morbidity/mortality in LMICs
key_findings: Long-term PM exposure associated with cardiovascular and respiratory morbidity/mortality in LMICs; PM1 effects understudied relative to PM2.5/PM10
limitations: LMIC studies underrepresented (only 38 of 1,978 initial hits met criteria); heterogeneous exposure assessment methods
rag_summary: LMIC-focused (relevant to India) systematic review confirming long-term PM exposure raises cardiovascular/respiratory disease risk, while flagging that finer PM1 particles remain understudied in these settings.
keywords: LMIC; PM1; PM2.5; PM10; cardiovascular; respiratory; air pollution

title: Relationship between fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentration and risk of hospitalization due to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: a systematic review and meta-analysis
variables: PM2.5 concentration; COPD hospitalization risk (odds ratio)
key_findings: Pooled analysis (19 studies) shows a significant association between PM2.5 exposure and increased COPD hospitalization risk
limitations: High heterogeneity across included studies (I2 = 94.86%); publication bias examined but residual bias possible
rag_summary: Confirms PM2.5 elevation is linked to increased COPD hospitalization risk, relevant to flagging respiratory-vulnerable users during poor-AQI periods.
keywords: PM2.5; COPD; hospitalization; respiratory disease

title: Epidemiological Association Between Long-Term Fine Particulate Matter Exposure and Cardiovascular Disease: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
population: 4 cohort studies, adults ≥15 years without baseline CVD
variables: Long-term PM2.5 exposure; CVD incidence, cardiovascular mortality, ischemic heart disease
key_findings: Increased CVD risk with long-term PM2.5 exposure (pooled HR 1.22, 95% CI 1.06-1.41); cardiovascular mortality and IHD associations were NOT statistically significant in this pooled analysis
limitations: Very small number of pooled studies (n=4); high heterogeneity (I2 up to 96%); non-significant findings for mortality/IHD should not be over-interpreted as 'no risk'
rag_summary: Important nuance: while overall CVD incidence rises with long-term PM2.5 exposure, this particular meta-analysis did NOT find a statistically significant link to cardiovascular mortality or ischemic heart disease specifically — illustrates why SwasthyaSathi must not claim mortality-level certainty from PM2.5 alone.
keywords: PM2.5; cardiovascular disease; ischemic heart disease; meta-analysis; non-significant

title: Sex Differences in Cardiovascular Risk Associated With Long-Term PM2.5 Exposure: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Cohort Studies
study_type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of cohort studies (PRISMA)
population: 25 cohort studies; 3.6M IHD and 1.3M stroke cases among 63.7M participants
variables: Long-term PM2.5; sex-specific IHD and stroke risk
key_findings: Long-term PM2.5 exposure associated with IHD and stroke in both sexes; explores possible (not conclusively proven) greater vulnerability in women via relative-risk-ratio comparisons
limitations: Sex-difference findings are exploratory/heterogeneous across cohorts; not a basis for individual-level sex-specific diagnosis
rag_summary: Large pooled cohort evidence linking long-term PM2.5 to ischemic heart disease and stroke, with exploratory (not definitive) evidence of sex-based differences in vulnerability.
keywords: PM2.5; sex differences; ischemic heart disease; stroke; cohort studies

title: Effect modification by sex for associations of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) with cardiovascular mortality, hospitalization, and emergency room visits: systematic review and meta-analysis
study_type: Systematic review and meta-analysis (GRADE quality rating)
variables: PM2.5; cardiovascular mortality, hospitalization, ER visits; sex as effect modifier
key_findings: Evidence for sex-differential cardiovascular risk from PM2.5 remains unclear/mixed after GRADE quality assessment
limitations: Explicitly flagged by the authors as producing unclear evidence for sex-based risk differences — should not be used to assert a definitive sex-specific risk claim
rag_summary: A caution-flag paper: despite pooling substantial data, evidence for whether men or women face higher PM2.5-cardiovascular risk remains genuinely unclear per GRADE assessment.
keywords: PM2.5; sex differences; cardiovascular mortality; GRADE; uncertain evidence

title: Association between PM2.5 and risk of hospitalization for myocardial infarction: a systematic review and a meta-analysis
variables: Short-term PM2.5 exposure; myocardial infarction hospitalization risk
key_findings: 10 µg/m3 increase in PM2.5 associated with RR = 1.02 (95% CI 1.01-1.03, p≤0.0001) for MI hospitalization — a small but statistically significant increase
limitations: Effect size is modest; residual confounding from co-pollutants and weather not fully addressed in all included studies
rag_summary: Quantifies a small but statistically robust increase in myocardial infarction hospitalization risk per 10 µg/m3 PM2.5 rise — useful for calibrating (not overstating) cardiac risk messaging tied to AQI spikes.
keywords: PM2.5; myocardial infarction; hospitalization; relative risk

title: PM2.5 and cardiovascular diseases: State-of-the-Art review
journal: ScienceDirect (journal not specified in retrieved excerpt)
population: Synthesis of cohort and meta-analytic studies
variables: PM2.5; arrhythmias (atrial fibrillation); stroke; broader cardiovascular disease spectrum
key_findings: Cites a meta-analysis of 16 cohort studies (>2.2M individuals) linking long-term PM2.5 to stroke; separately notes PM2.5 associated with increased atrial fibrillation risk (~22% in one Taiwan study)
limitations: Narrative review format — not itself a primary systematic review; individual cited effect sizes vary by study design
rag_summary: Broad review connecting PM2.5 to a wider cardiovascular spectrum including stroke and atrial fibrillation, beyond the more commonly cited MI/CVD mortality endpoints.
keywords: PM2.5; atrial fibrillation; stroke; cardiovascular disease; review

title: Air Pollution and Headache Disorders
journal: Annals of Indian Academy of Neurology
population: Synthesis of epidemiological and clinical studies
variables: Air pollution (NO2, CO, PM); headache and migraine disorders
key_findings: Air pollution is associated with several neurological disorders including headache/migraine, plausibly via oxidative stress and neurogenic inflammation pathways
limitations: Narrative (non-systematic) review; causal mechanism proposed but not definitively established; published in an Indian neurology journal, giving some regional relevance
rag_summary: India-published review linking ambient air pollution to headache/migraine disorders — useful evidence base for AQI-linked headache-symptom flags, with appropriate caution about correlational strength.
keywords: air pollution; headache; migraine; neurological disorders; India

title: The association between ambient air pollution and migraine: a systematic review
population: 14 of 1,417 identified articles met inclusion criteria
variables: NO2, CO, PM2.5, PM10; migraine occurrence
key_findings: NO2 (78.3% of relationships) and CO (68.0%) most consistently associated with migraine triggering among gaseous pollutants; evidence needs confirmation in larger studies
limitations: Only 14 studies met inclusion criteria out of 1,417 screened; authors explicitly state findings need confirmation in larger-scale studies
rag_summary: Systematic review finding a plausible but not yet firmly confirmed link between NO2/CO exposure and migraine — should be presented as suggestive, not conclusive, evidence.
keywords: air pollution; migraine; NO2; carbon monoxide; systematic review

title: Evaluating the Accuracy of Low-Cost Wearable Sensors for Healthcare Monitoring
variables: Heart rate; SpO2; blood pressure trend; body temperature via PPG/IR wearable prototype
key_findings: Bland-Altman analysis found clinically acceptable agreement thresholds (±5mmHg BP, ±5-10bpm HR, ±4% SpO2, ±0.5°C temp) versus validated commercial devices
limitations: Very small sample (n=10); prototype device, not commercially validated at scale; short monitoring window
rag_summary: Small validation study showing low-cost wearable prototypes can achieve clinically acceptable accuracy for HR, SpO2, BP-trend and temperature — relevant baseline for SwasthyaSathi's sensor accuracy claims, with the caveat of small sample size.
keywords: wearable sensor; heart rate; SpO2; validation; Bland-Altman

title: Assessment of Physiological Signals from Photoplethysmography Sensors Compared to an Electrocardiogram Sensor: A Validation Study in Daily Life
variables: PPG-derived heart rate (HR) and HRV vs ECG reference
key_findings: PPG-derived HR/HRV showed reasonable accuracy (mean absolute error <1 bpm for HR, 6-15ms for HRV), best during sleep; accuracy degraded during activity (14-51% higher relative error)
limitations: Healthy volunteers only; accuracy substantially reduced during movement/activity, a key limitation for real-world continuous monitoring
rag_summary: Establishes that consumer PPG wearables are reasonably accurate for HR/HRV at rest/sleep but notably less reliable during activity — important for SwasthyaSathi to avoid over-trusting vitals during active outdoor exposure.
keywords: PPG; ECG; heart rate variability; validation; free-living

title: Continuous Monitoring of Heart Rate Variability in Free-Living Conditions Using Wearable Sensors: Exploratory Observational Study
authors: Pooja Gaur; Dorota S Temple; Meghan Hegarty-Craver; Matthew D Boyce; Jonathan R Holt; Michael F Wenger; Edward A Preble; Randall P Eckhoff; Michelle S McCombs; Hope C Davis-Wilson; Howard J Walls; David E Dausch
journal: JMIR (exact sub-journal not specified in excerpt)
population: 59 participants, 8-month continuous monitoring via Garmin Fenix 6 smartwatches
variables: Interbeat interval (HRV); step count; self-reported symptoms/illness (respiratory infection focus)
key_findings: Demonstrates feasibility of an automated pipeline computing 'health risk scores' from continuous HRV/activity data linked to self-reported illness over an 8-month free-living period
limitations: Exploratory design, not a validated diagnostic tool; illness labels are self-reported, introducing recall/reporting bias
rag_summary: Real-world (59-participant, 8-month) proof-of-concept that continuous wearable HRV monitoring combined with symptom logging can generate meaningful 'health risk' signals — directly analogous to SwasthyaSathi's personalization/baseline-learning goal.
keywords: heart rate variability; wearable; free-living; respiratory illness; health risk score

title: The Sunrise SpO2 and Pulse Rate Accuracy Validation Study
variables: SpO2 accuracy (ARMS) vs arterial blood CO-oximetry; pulse rate accuracy vs ECG
key_findings: Trial protocol targets ARMS ≤3.5% accuracy standard for reflectance pulse oximetry across 70-100% SaO2 range
limitations: This is a trial registration record, not a completed results publication — outcomes not yet confirmed in this source
rag_summary: Illustrates the rigorous clinical validation standard (ARMS ≤3.5%) that pulse-oximetry sensors must meet against arterial blood gold-standard — a useful accuracy benchmark to cite (not a completed-results source).
keywords: SpO2; pulse oximetry; accuracy validation; ARMS; clinical trial

title: Validation of nocturnal resting heart rate and heart rate variability in consumer wearables
authors: Michael B. Dial; Margaret E. Hollander; Emaly A. Vatne; Angela M. Emerson; Nathan A. Edwards; Joshua A. Hagen
variables: Nocturnal resting heart rate; HRV from consumer wearables
key_findings: Assesses validity of consumer wearable nocturnal HR/HRV metrics for potential clinical/monitoring use in cardiovascular disease, stress, and sleep-disorder populations
limitations: Focused on nocturnal metrics only; generalizability to daytime/active monitoring not addressed
rag_summary: 2025 validation study specifically on nighttime HR/HRV metrics from consumer wearables, relevant for baseline-establishment during rest/sleep in SwasthyaSathi's personalization engine.
keywords: heart rate variability; nocturnal; consumer wearables; validation

title: A guide to consumer-grade wearables in cardiovascular clinical care and population health for non-experts
variables: SpO2, step count, HR from consumer wearables; agreement with medical-grade devices
key_findings: SpO2 agreement with medical-grade pulse oximeters ranges from -2.7% to +5.9% (95% limits of agreement), with outliers up to 15%; frequent SpO2 underestimation noted in some devices
limitations: Consumer SpO2 accuracy varies substantially by device and skin/perfusion conditions; not validated for clinical diagnosis in patients with existing oxygenation disorders
rag_summary: Important caution: consumer wearable SpO2 readings can deviate up to 15% from medical-grade values, meaning SwasthyaSathi should treat wearable SpO2 as a directional/trend signal, not a diagnostic-grade measurement.
keywords: consumer wearables; SpO2 accuracy; cardiovascular; population health

title: State-of-the-art wearable sensors for cardiovascular health: a review
variables: PPG sensor design (transmission vs reflection mode); heart rate; SpO2; pulse waveform
key_findings: Transmission-mode PPG (finger/ear clips) provides higher signal-to-noise ratio and better accuracy for SpO2/HR than reflection-mode (wrist) sensors, especially under low perfusion
limitations: Technical/engineering review, not a clinical outcomes study
rag_summary: Explains why sensor placement (finger/ear vs wrist) affects PPG-based HR/SpO2 accuracy — technically relevant for hardware design choices in the SwasthyaSathi wearable.
keywords: PPG; sensor design; wearable; SpO2; heart rate

title: Does increased core temperature alter cognitive performance during exercise-induced heat strain? A narrative review
variables: Core body temperature; cognitive performance (reaction time, memory, Stroop task); dehydration
key_findings: Core temperature alone is not a sufficient predictor of cognitive impairment; reaction time, memory recall and Stroop-task performance are most sensitive to combined heat+dehydration strain
limitations: Evidence is 'equivocal' per the authors; heterogeneous exercise protocols and cognitive tests across studies limit direct comparison
rag_summary: Important nuance for symptom logic: rising core temperature alone does NOT reliably predict cognitive/fatigue symptoms — combined physiological stressors (temperature + dehydration + exertion) matter more, so SwasthyaSathi should avoid single-variable causal claims about heat and cognitive symptoms.
keywords: core temperature; cognitive performance; heat strain; dehydration; narrative review

title: Effects of heat strain on cognitive function among a sample of miners
variables: Heat stress (37.8°C); reaction time; Stroop effect; verbal memory; working memory
key_findings: Heat stress impaired serial reaction time, Stroop-task inhibition, and delayed memory; did NOT significantly affect continuous working memory (N-back) task
limitations: Very small sample (n=8); participants did not show clear dehydration, limiting ability to isolate heat vs. dehydration effects
rag_summary: Small controlled study showing heat stress selectively impairs some cognitive domains (reaction time, memory recall) but not others (working memory) — evidence that symptom relationships with heat are task/domain-specific, not uniform.
keywords: heat stress; cognitive function; reaction time; working memory; occupational

title: High prevalence of hypohydration in occupations with heat stress—Perspectives for performance in combined cognitive and motor tasks
study_type: Mixed occupational survey + controlled crossover laboratory study
population: 139 workers (5 European industries) for hydration survey; 8 male participants for lab crossover
variables: Urine specific gravity (dehydration marker); core temperature elevation (1°C, 2°C); cognitive and motor task performance
key_findings: Dehydration (~2% bodyweight deficit) aggravates the impact of hyperthermia on combined cognitive-motor task performance beyond either factor alone
limitations: Lab sample very small (n=8, male only); occupational hydration survey and lab experiment are separate populations, not directly linked
rag_summary: Shows dehydration and heat interact synergistically to impair cognitive-motor performance — supports combined (not siloed) risk scoring for heat + hydration status rather than treating them as independent symptom triggers.
keywords: hypohydration; heat stress; cognitive-motor performance; occupational health

title: Effects of heat stress and dehydration on cognitive function in elite female field hockey players
variables: Exercise-induced dehydration (~2% body mass loss); working memory; vigilance; Stroop test
key_findings: Mixed/inconsistent findings on hypohydration's effect on cognition; complex Stroop-test performance actually improved in this cohort, contrasting with some other studies
limitations: Small elite-athlete sample not generalizable to general population or non-exercise heat exposure; findings partly contradict other heat-cognition studies, illustrating evidence inconsistency
rag_summary: Demonstrates that dehydration's effect on cognition is inconsistent across studies (this one found improved, not impaired, complex-task performance) — key evidence that SwasthyaSathi should NOT assert dehydration always causes cognitive symptoms.
keywords: dehydration; cognitive function; athletes; inconsistent evidence

title: Heat Stroke
variables: Body temperature >40°C; CNS dysfunction (confusion, ataxia, delirium, seizures); heat exhaustion vs heat stroke continuum
key_findings: Heat exhaustion symptoms: cramping, fatigue, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, headache. Heat stroke is distinguished by CNS dysfunction and typically (not always) >40°C body temperature
limitations: Educational/reference source, not a primary research study; clinical thresholds are guidelines, not universal cutoffs
rag_summary: Authoritative NIH clinical reference distinguishing heat exhaustion (cramping, fatigue, dizziness, nausea, headache) from heat stroke (CNS dysfunction plus high temperature) — core symptom taxonomy for SwasthyaSathi's risk-tiering logic.
keywords: heat stroke; heat exhaustion; CNS dysfunction; clinical reference

title: Exertional heat stroke: an evidence based approach to clinical assessment and management
variables: Exertional heat stroke; CNS dysfunction; field cooling; AVPU vital signs assessment
key_findings: Prompt recognition and aggressive field cooling substantially reduce morbidity/mortality from exertional heat stroke; describes continuum-of-care from field to hospital
limitations: Focused on exertional (physical activity-induced) heat stroke, which may differ mechanistically from classic/passive heat stroke in the elderly
rag_summary: Evidence-based clinical management pathway for exertional heat stroke, useful for structuring SwasthyaSathi's SOS/emergency escalation logic (recognition → field cooling → transport).
keywords: exertional heat stroke; field cooling; clinical management; emergency

title: Exertional Heat Stroke and Rhabdomyolysis: A Medical Record Review and Patient Perspective on Management and Long-Term Symptoms
authors: Nick Kruijt; L. R. van den Bersselaar; M. T. E. Hopman; M. M. J. Snoeck; M. van Rijswick; T. G. H. Wiggers; H. Jungbluth; C. C. W. G. Bongers; N. C. Voermans
study_type: Prospective survey + retrospective medical record review
variables: Exertional heat stroke/rhabdomyolysis; prehospital management; long-term (6/12-month) mental health outcomes
key_findings: Prehospital management was inconsistent with guidelines in the majority of cases; self-reported risk factors included poor heat acclimatization (55%) and peer pressure (28%)
limitations: Self-reported survey component subject to recall bias; Netherlands-specific cohort, not necessarily representative of tropical/Indian heat exposure contexts
rag_summary: Real-world evidence that prehospital heat-stroke management is frequently inconsistent with guidelines, and that poor acclimatization is a major modifiable risk factor — supports SwasthyaSathi's acclimatization-aware personalization.
keywords: exertional heat stroke; rhabdomyolysis; acclimatization; prehospital management

title: Heat-Related Illness (Recognition: Heat Exhaustion)
journal: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)
variables: Heat exhaustion warning signs; progression risk to heat stroke
key_findings: Heat exhaustion signs: heavy sweating, paleness, muscle cramps, tiredness, weakness, dizziness, headache, nausea/vomiting, fainting, cool/moist skin, fast/weak pulse, fast/shallow breathing
limitations: Public health guidance document, not a primary research study; general population guidance, not individualized risk stratification
rag_summary: Authoritative CDC symptom checklist for heat exhaustion — directly usable as the canonical symptom list for SwasthyaSathi's heat-related symptom-matching logic.
keywords: heat exhaustion; CDC; symptom recognition; public health guidance

title: Short-term environmental nitrogen dioxide exposure and neurology clinic visits for headaches, a time-series study in Wuhan, China
population: 11,436 neurology clinic visit records, Wuhan, China, Jan 2017-Nov 2019
variables: Ambient NO2 concentration; neurology clinic visits for headache
key_findings: A 10 µg/m3 increase in NO2 corresponded to a 3.64% increase in daily headache-related neurology clinic visits (95% CI 1.02-6.32%, p=0.006)
limitations: Single-city (China) ecological time-series design cannot establish individual-level causation; unmeasured co-pollutants/weather confounders possible
rag_summary: Quantifies a modest but statistically significant association between short-term NO2 spikes and headache-related clinic visits — supports (with appropriate caveats) linking AQI/NO2 alerts to headache-symptom risk flags.
keywords: nitrogen dioxide; headache; time-series; air pollution; clinic visits

title: Accuracy of Triage Systems in Disasters and Mass Casualty Incidents; a Systematic Review
authors: Jafar Bazyar; Mehrdad Farrokhi; Amir Salari; Hamid Safarpour; Hamid Reza Khankeh
population: Global triage systems (START, mSTART, SALT, Smart, CareFlight, ASAV, MPTT, Sieve, ESI)
variables: Triage system type; accuracy, sensitivity, specificity in disasters/mass casualty incidents
